title: I Took the Public Chess-Clock Policy to the Club Prez Who Used Analog

parts.text: I sat table two at 1:03 p.m. and prez Nell started an analog clock under the digital rule. The plaque said: PUBLIC CLOCKS. FIVE PLUS THREE. NO PERSONAL TIMERS. I was thirty-three, park player, holding a laminated card. Nell shrugged. "Presidents are the tempo." I photographed the plaque, the analog, and her flag. Then I asked for the table log. At 1:09 parks staff pinged why Nell's analog was on a public table. I did not argue the joke. I argued the file. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: Parks staff can see Nell's analog timer on table two under the digital plaque.

social.video_title: The club prez ran analog on a public digital table — Part 1/2
social.description: Park chess, a personal timer, a five-plus-three plaque. I logged the flag. Would you have asked for the table log?

parts.text: Nell called it tradition until parks asked for the still. I printed the log, the plaque, and the photo. The analog went in her bag. Nell ran five-plus-three like everyone else and told the next prez tempo was always about optics. Optics is a word presidents use when a plaque exists. Clock policy now has a second line: PERSONAL TIMERS ARE NOT PUBLIC. I keep the laminated card. Nell brown-bags her jokes. The table finally looks like a park, not a clubhouse. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Personal timers are not public — Part 2/2
social.description: Table log, bagged analog, and a second line on the plaque. Was tradition ever the park?
